title: Donald Knuth’s “Claude’s Cycles”: Claude Opus 4.6 Solves Open 3D Directed Hamiltonian Cycle Decomposition
whyItMatters: Computer science legend Donald Knuth titled his paper “Claude’s Cycles” after Claude Opus 4.6 solved an open 3D Cayley-digraph Hamiltonian decomposition problem he had been working on for The Art of Computer Programming.
summary: On February 28, 2026, Stanford professor emeritus Donald E. Knuth published a celebrated paper titled “Claude’s Cycles,” opening with shock after Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 (coached by Filip Stappers) cracked an open graph-theory problem Knuth had been studying for weeks for a future volume of The Art of Computer Programming. Given the m×m×m directed 3D toroidal grid Cayley digraph where each vertex (i, j, k) has three outgoing arcs incrementing one coordinate mod m, the problem asked for a general rule decomposing all 3m³ arcs into three directed Hamiltonian cycles for every odd m > 1. Claude explored small cases systematically via code and discovered a remarkably simple closed-form “bumping” rule; Knuth proved its correctness for all odd m, and the Lean community (Kim Morrison) promptly machine-verified the theorem in Lean 4.
technicalHighlights: Claude Opus 4.6 systematically explored small m cases with self-written programs to uncover a clean closed-form Hamiltonian-cycle decomposition rule for all odd m > 1.
Donald Knuth independently verified and proved the general construction, publishing the landmark paper “Claude’s Cycles” (Stanford CS, Feb 28, 2026).
Formally verified in Lean 4 shortly after release (github.com/kim-em/KnuthClaudeLean).
caveats: Claude discovered the constructive decomposition rule for all odd m while Donald Knuth supplied the full human proof of generality (and the even-m case remained separate).

scoreRationale.foundational: Solved a crisp open combinatorial decomposition problem directly slated for Knuth’s canonical Art of Computer Programming.
scoreRationale.ripple: Endorsement by Donald Knuth himself became one of the most influential cultural and scientific validation moments for AI-assisted mathematics and computer science.
scoreRationale.verification: Proved rigorously by Donald Knuth and independently machine-checked in Lean 4.
scoreRationale.velocity: Uncovered a general constructive rule in roughly one hour of interactive exploration after weeks of human effort.
